questions.stem: The ionic equation for neutralisation is H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l). What does this tell us about what actually reacts during neutralisation?

options.text: The metal ions and acid ions react together
Only the hydrogen ions from the acid and hydroxide ions from the alkali react to form water
All ions in solution react
The water molecules split apart

questions.explanation: The ionic equation shows that neutralisation is specifically the reaction between H+ ions (from the acid) and OH- ions (from the alkali) to form water. The other ions (e.g., Na+, Cl-) are spectator ions that do not participate in the reaction. This is why all strong acid-strong alkali neutralisations have the same enthalpy change.

questions.stem: A farmer spreads calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) on fields that have acidic soil. What type of reaction occurs and why is it beneficial?

options.text: Combustion - the lime burns the excess acid
Neutralisation - the calcium hydroxide reacts with the acid to raise the soil pH towards neutral
Oxidation - the lime adds oxygen to the soil
Decomposition - the lime breaks down the acid molecules

questions.explanation: Calcium hydroxide is a base that neutralises the excess acid in the soil. Ca(OH)2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2H2O (for example). This raises the pH towards neutral, which is important because most crops grow best in soil that is close to neutral (pH 6-7). This is a practical application of neutralisation in agriculture.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. If sulfuric acid is used instead of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, what salt is produced?

options.text: Sodium chloride
Sodium nitrate
Sodium sulfate
Sodium carbonate

questions.explanation: The salt produced depends on the acid used: HCl produces chlorides, H2SO4 produces sulfates, and HNO3 produces nitrates. The metal comes from the base/alkali. So: H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Sodium sulfate is the salt produced. Note that sulfuric acid is diprotic, so it needs 2 NaOH to neutralise.

questions.stem: A wasp sting is alkaline (contains a base). What would be an appropriate household remedy to apply?

options.text: Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate), which is alkaline
Toothpaste, which is alkaline
Vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid), which would neutralise the alkaline sting
Soap, which is alkaline

questions.explanation: Since wasp stings are alkaline, a weak acid should be applied to neutralise them. Vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid) would neutralise the base in the sting. Applying an alkali (baking soda, toothpaste, or soap) would not help because these are also basic/alkaline and would not neutralise the sting. (By contrast, bee stings are acidic and can be treated with baking soda.)

questions.stem: During a neutralisation reaction in a polystyrene cup, the temperature rises from 22°C to 35°C. What does this temperature change tell us about neutralisation?

options.text: Neutralisation is an endothermic reaction
Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction - energy is released to the surroundings
The temperature rise is caused by mixing, not the reaction
Neutralisation has no energy change

questions.explanation: The temperature rise of 13°C shows that neutralisation is an exothermic reaction - energy is released as thermal energy. When H+ ions combine with OH- ions to form water, energy is released because the O-H bonds in water are very stable (low energy). This is why all strong acid-strong alkali neutralisations release about 57.1 kJ/mol.
